title: Electric potential energy of a two-charge system
body: The work required for an external force to bring the point charges to their current positions from infinitely far away.
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.1: "equals the amount of work required for an external force to bring the point charges to their current positions from infinitely far away"

title: Electric potential energy of two point charges
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.2: "general form for the electric potential energy between two charged objects"

title: Total potential energy of a multi-charge system
caution: Count each pair of charges exactly once.
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.3: "sum of the electric potential energies of the individual interactions between each pair of charged objects"

title: Electric potential
body: The electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in space.
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.1: "Electric potential describes the electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in space"

title: Potential from a charge distribution (integration)
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.2: "found using integration and the principle of superposition"

title: Electric potential of a single point charge
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.2.i: "The electric potential for single point charge"

title: Potential of multiple point charges
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.2.ii: "principle of scalar superposition of the electric potential"

title: Potential adds as a scalar; field adds as a vector
body: Superpose electric potential by scalar addition (signs of charges matter, direction does not), unlike electric field, which requires vector addition.
caution: Say 'scalar superposition' for V; do not add components or directions for V.

title: Electric potential difference
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.3: "change in electric potential energy per unit charge when a test charge is moved between the two points"

title: Electric field from potential
ced_evidence: 9.2.B.1: "negative of the spatial rate of change in electric potential"

title: Potential difference from field (line integral)
caution: Use the correct pair of endpoints as limits; substitute the field expression into the integral.
ced_evidence: 9.2.B.2: "integrating the dot product of the electric field and the displacement along the path"

title: Equipotential line (isoline)
body: A line of equal electric potential, also called an isoline of electric potential.
ced_evidence: 9.2.B.3.i: "Equipotential lines represent lines of equal electric potential"

title: Isolines are perpendicular to the electric field
body: Isolines are perpendicular to electric field vectors, so there is no field component along an isoline, and either map can be constructed from the other.
ced_evidence: 9.2.B.3.ii, 9.2.B.3.iv: "Isolines are perpendicular to electric field vectors"

title: Field direction relative to potential
body: An electric field vector points in the direction of decreasing potential.
ced_evidence: 9.2.B.3.iii: "points in the direction of decreasing potential"

title: Change in potential energy of a charge moving through a potential difference
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.1: "resulting change in the electric potential energy of the object-field system"

title: Energy conservation for a charge in a potential difference
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.2: "change in kinetic energy of the object consistent with the conservation of energy"
